title: Creating Exercises
text: The quarto-live extension allows you to define a collection of linked code cells and blocks to form an exercise. An exercise is fundamentally an interactive code block, but with the addition of optional setup code, hints, solutions, and grading.

title: Creating Exercises
text:
Create an Exercise
To designate a webr block as an exercise set the exercise cell option, giving it a unique label. Later we will link additional features to the exercise by referring to this label.

Source


exercise.qmd

Fill in the blank so that the result of the sum is 10.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
1 + 2 + 3 + ______
```



Output
Fill in the blank so that the result of the sum is 10.








Exercises may optionally include a series of six or more underscores, designated as “blanks”. The learner will be prompted to replace the blanks with code when evaluating an exercise.






Note



Unlike standard interactive code blocks, exercises do not auto-evaluate by default – the “Run Code” button must be activated by the learner to evaluate the code.

title: Creating Exercises
text:
Running setup code
Often you will want to run some setup code in preparation for your exercise. For example, you might want to ensure a package is available, or prepare for some data to be used in the exercise.
Designate a webr block as an exercise setup block by setting the setup: true cell option. Then, set the exercise cell option so as to match an existing exercise. The code in the exercise setup cell will be executed before every evaluation of the learner’s code.

Source
Fill in the blank so that the result of the sum is 10.


exercise.qmd

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_2
foo <- 1
bar <- 2
baz <- 3
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
foo + bar + baz + ______
```



Output
Fill in the blank so that the result of the sum is 10.













Shared setup
A setup block may be attached to multiple exercises by providing a list of exercises for the exercise cell option. The code in the setup cell will be executed before every evaluation of any of the listed exercises.

Source


exercise.qmd

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|   - ex_a1
#|   - ex_a2
var_xyz <- c(1, 3, 7, 9, 13, 15)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_a1
var_xyz * 2
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_a2
var_xyz ** 2
```



Output

title: Creating Exercises
text:
Adding hints and solutions
Add hints and solutions to your exercise in the form of fenced blocks. The blocks should set the .hint or .solution class. Then, link the blocks to your exercise by setting the exercise attribute.
Linked exercises will display UI button elements to reveal hints and solutions. Multiple hints and solutions blocks can be linked; hints will be revealed progressively and all solutions at once.

Source


exercise.qmd

Filter the `starwars` dataset so that only the droid characters are included.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_3
library(dplyr)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
starwars |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_3"}
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

Consider using the `filter()` function from `dplyr`.

```r
starwars |> filter(______)
```
:::
:::

::: { .hint exercise="ex_3"}
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

You should filter the dataset using the `species` column.

```r

```
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_3" }

Use the `filter()` function from `dplyr`:

```r
starwars |>                                 #<1>
    filter(species == "Droid")              #<2>
```
1. Take the `starwars` dataset, and then,
2. Filter for the "Droid" species.

:::

live:

title: Managing Environments
text:
For a standard (non-exercise) interactive code block, the default environment label is "global", meaning “the global environment”. That means that variables put into the environment in one executable code block can be accessed in by blocks that are subsequently evaluated.


Source

```{webr}
# Assignment in non-exercise blocks is in the global environment
foo <- c(1, 3, 5, 7)
```

```{webr}
# So, non-exercise blocks can share variables
foo + 42
```

title: Managing Environments
text:
For a standard (non-exercise) interactive code block, the default environment label is "global", meaning “the global environment”. That means that variables put into the environment in one executable code block can be accessed in by blocks that are subsequently evaluated.


Source

```{webr}
# Assignment in non-exercise blocks is in the global environment
foo <- c(1, 3, 5, 7)
```

```{webr}
# So, non-exercise blocks can share variables
foo + 42
```

title: Managing Environments
text:
Exercise environments
On the other hand, we often want to ensure that exercises do not interfere with one another. As such, each exercise is given a unique environment for evaluation. Exercises can access variables defined in the global environment, but not the other way around.


Source

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
#| setup: true
# Assignment in setup blocks are put into the exercise environment
bar <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
#| autorun: true
# Exercises variables in both their own and the global environment
foo
bar
```

```{webr}
# Evaluation in the global environment cannot see variables
# defined in exercise environments
bar
```

title: Managing Environments
text:
Manually managing the environment
Environments can be managed manually, if you wish, by setting the envir cell option to a shared label. Exercises sharing the same environment label are all executed in the same environment. This can be used to create “follow-on” exercises.


Source

```{webr}
#| envir: myenv
#| exercise: ex_shared_1
#| autorun: true
abc <- 7
```

```{webr}
#| envir: myenv
#| exercise: ex_shared_2
#| autorun: true
xyz <- 5
```

```{webr}
#| envir: myenv
#| exercise: ex_shared_3
#| autorun: true
abc + xyz
```


























Example: Shared environments with grading


Source

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_shared_1a
dataset <- data.frame(foo = c(1,2,3), bar = c(10,100,1000))
my_mean <- NULL
```

#### Exercise 1a

The `dataset` variable has been created in a `setup: true` block.

Calculate the mean of the `foo` column in `dataset`. Save the result as `my_mean`.

```{webr}
#| envir: myenv
#| exercise: ex_shared_1a
my_mean <- ______(dataset$foo)
```

```{webr}
#| check: true
#| exercise: ex_shared_1a
if (identical(my_mean, mean(dataset$foo))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Nice work!")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's incorrect, sorry.")
}
```

#### Exercise 1b

The `dataset` variable is also accessible from this exercise, because both exercises have the `envir: myenv` option set.

Calculate the standard deviation of the `bar` column in `dataset`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_shared_1b
#| envir: myenv
sd(______)
```

```{webr}
#| check: true
#| exercise: ex_shared_1b
if (identical(.result, sd(dataset$bar))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Nice work!")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's incorrect, sorry.")
}
```





Exercise 1a
The dataset variable has been created in a setup: true block.
Calculate the mean of the foo column in dataset. Save the result as my_mean.













Exercise 1b
The dataset variable is also accessible from this exercise, because both exercises have the envir: myenv option set.
Calculate the standard deviation of the bar column in dataset.

text:
A normal SQL block without exercise uses the default environment global.
This means that one SQL block can create tables, and later SQL blocks can use the same tables again. In this first block, we create two global tables: foo and bar.






The next SQL block can access foo, because it was created in the global environment above.

text:
Exercise isolation from global
Normal SQL blocks and exercise SQL blocks should not always share the same state.
The table people was created in the global environment. This exercise uses its own exercise environment, so it should not see people.






Expected result: this block should show an error, because people does not exist inside this exercise environment.

Manually managing the environment
Sometimes exercises should build on each other. Quarto Live supports this with the envir option.
Exercises with the same manual envir value share the same environment. This can be used for follow-on exercises.

Follow-on exercise 1
This exercise creates a table and inserts one value.








Follow-on exercise 2

Follow-on exercise 3

Expected result: the total should be 12.

title: SQL Grading Test
text:
Test 1: Correct solution passes check
This test verifies that setup code creates the initial table, the exercise modifies the database state, and the check evaluates the resulting state.








Expected result: The check should pass, because the table contains exactly three rows.

Expected result: The check should fail, because the table contains only one row instead of three.

title: SQL Functional Tests
text:
This document contains functional tests for the SQL extension. The tests correspond to the feature matrix and cover client-side execution, static delivery, normal SQL blocks, editor options, isolated exercises, shared environments, setup and grading, error feedback, schema-aware autocomplete, psql-style meta commands, meta-command autocomplete, and autorun.
The tests are intended to be executed in the rendered HTML document. Unless stated otherwise, editable SQL blocks should be executed manually with Run Code.

section: Test 2: Normal SQL blocks, global state, tabular output, and before-all behavior
text:
Test 2: Normal SQL blocks, global state, tabular output, and before-all behavior
This test verifies that normal SQL blocks share a global database state. A table created in one normal SQL block should be available in later normal SQL blocks. This also demonstrates that a normal SQL block can function as a document-wide preparation step comparable to a limited before-all mechanism when executed before later blocks.












Expected result: After running the blocks in order, the final SELECT output is displayed as a table with the columns id and value and contains three rows.

title: SQL Functional Tests
text:
Test 3: Isolated exercises
This test verifies that SQL exercises without a shared envir use separate database states. Two exercises use the same table name but should not interfere with each other.
















Expected result: The first exercise contains two rows after execution. The second exercise contains only its own setup row. This shows that the exercises do not accidentally share the same database state.

This test verifies that multiple exercises with the same envir option share one database state. The first exercise creates the table, and later exercises use and extend the same state.



















Expected result: After running the shared exercises in order, the shared environment contains both inserted rows. The check for shared_three passes because all exercises use the same envir.

section: Test 6: SQL editor, schema-aware autocomplete, and autorun
text:
Test 6: SQL editor, schema-aware autocomplete, and autorun
This test verifies editor-based SQL input, schema-aware autocomplete, and the Quarto Live editor option autorun.

Test 6.1: Schema-aware autocomplete
This test verifies that the SQL editor can suggest table and column names from the current PGlite schema.

Source


sql-functional-test.qmd

```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autocomplete
#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS autocomplete_items;

CREATE TABLE autocomplete_items (
  id INTEGER,
  label TEXT,
  amount INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO autocomplete_items VALUES
  (1, 'first', 10),
  (2, 'second', 20);
```









Expected result: The SQL editor should suggest the table autocomplete_items and the columns id, label, and amount. The query should return two rows and the check should pass.



Test 6.2: Autorun in SQL editor
This test verifies that an editable SQL block with autorun: true is executed automatically when the editor is initialized.

Source


sql-functional-test.qmd

```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autorun
#| autorun: true

INSERT INTO autorun_editor VALUES
  (1, 'created by editor autorun');

SELECT *
FROM autorun_editor;
```









Expected result: The SQL block with autorun: true is executed automatically without pressing the run button. The output displays the inserted row and the check passes.

text:
Test 7: Editor option combinations
This test verifies the interaction between edit and autorun. The options affect different aspects of execution: edit controls whether an editor is shown, while autorun controls whether an editable block is executed automatically during initialization.

Test 7.1: edit: true, autorun: false
This test verifies the default interactive editor behavior. The editor should be visible, but the SQL code should not be executed until Run Code is pressed.






Expected result: An editor is displayed. No result should be shown until Run Code is pressed. After execution, the output contains the value manual editor execution.


Test 7.2: edit: true, autorun: true
This test verifies automatic execution of an editable non-exercise SQL block.






Expected result: An editor is displayed and the SQL code is executed automatically during initialization. The output contains the value automatic editor execution without pressing Run Code.


Test 7.3: edit: false, autorun: false
This test verifies non-editable SQL block behavior. Since the block is not editable, no editor should be shown. The block should be evaluated directly.






Expected result: No editor is displayed. The output is shown directly and contains the value direct evaluation without editor.


Test 7.4: edit: false, autorun: true
This test verifies that edit: false selects the non-interactive evaluation path. In this case, autorun is not the relevant trigger because no editor is created.






Expected result: No editor is displayed. The block is evaluated directly. The result contains the value direct evaluation ignores editor autorun.

title: SQL Functional Tests

Test 8: Psql-style meta commands
This test verifies that psql-style meta commands are recognized by the SQL evaluator and executed through the current PGlite environment.






























Expected result: The command \? displays help output. The command \dt lists the table students. The command \d students displays information about the columns of the table. The command \du is recognized as a supported meta command and returns the role information available in the current PGlite environment.

This test verifies that the SQL editor suggests supported psql-style meta commands.






Expected result: When typing \ or \d in the SQL editor, the editor suggests supported meta commands such as \dt, \du, and \d. Executing \dt runs the meta command through the SQL evaluator.

title: SQL Functional Tests
section: Test 11: Meta commands as standalone input
text:
Test 11: Meta commands as standalone input
This test documents the expected boundary of psql-style meta commands. Meta commands are treated as standalone inputs and should not be mixed with SQL statements in the same block.






Expected result: Regular SQL executes normally. Meta commands such as \dt should be used as separate editor input, not mixed with SQL statements in the same block.

title: SQL Functional Tests
text:
This test verifies that SQL statements are executed client-side through PGlite in the browser, without an external SQL server. It covers basic execution, PostgreSQL type enforcement, multi-statement blocks, and error handling.


This test verifies that a table created in one block is accessible in a later block, confirming that the global database state persists across normal SQL blocks.












Expected result: The second block displays two rows with the values inserted in the first block.




This test verifies that PGlite enforces PostgreSQL column types strictly. Inserting a string into an INTEGER column should produce a type error, confirming that PGlite behaves like PostgreSQL and not like SQLite, which accepts such inserts silently.






Expected result: The block produces a type error. The error is displayed as feedback in the document and does not cause an uncaught browser crash.




This test verifies that a single SQL block can contain multiple statements. PGlite executes all statements sequentially, and the last statement with rows is shown as output.






Expected result: The block executes all four statements. The output shows the three inserted rows as a table.




This test verifies that a malformed SQL statement is caught by the evaluator and shown as feedback, without causing an uncaught JavaScript error or crashing the page.






Expected result: The error message relation "table_that_does_not_exist" does not exist is displayed as feedback. The rest of the page remains functional.

Test 2: Global state isolation and tabular output
This test verifies that the global database state is isolated from exercise environments, and that tabular output correctly renders different PostgreSQL data types.

Test 2.1: Global state is isolated from exercise environments

Expected result: The exercise block can access exercise_only but not global_only. The global block can access global_only. The check passes because global_only is not visible inside the exercise environment.



Test 2.2: Tabular output with multiple PostgreSQL data types

Expected result: The output table shows three rows with all four columns correctly rendered. Boolean values appear as true or false, and numeric values show two decimal places.

section: Test 5: Start Over resets state and replays setup
text:
Test 5: Start Over resets state and replays setup
This test verifies that clicking Start Over resets the editor content to the original code and replays the setup block, restoring the exercise to its initial state.








Expected result: After running the exercise block, the table contains two rows and the check passes. After clicking Start Over, the editor resets to the original code and the setup is replayed. Running the block again should again produce two rows, confirming that the state was cleanly reset.

title: SQL Exercise Tests
section: Test 2: SQL exercises are fully isolated from the global database
text:
Test 2: SQL exercises are fully isolated from the global database
This test verifies that SQL exercises cannot access tables created in normal global SQL blocks. Unlike WebR and Python exercises, each SQL exercise uses its own dedicated PGlite instance. This means that global SQL blocks and exercise blocks do not share the same database state, even when given the same envir label.












Expected result: The exercise block produces the error relation "global_ref" does not exist. This confirms that SQL exercises are fully isolated from the global database state. The correct way to prepare data for an exercise is to use a setup: true block, not a global SQL block.

title: SQL Exercise Tests
section: Test 3: Setup block is the correct way to share data with exercises
text:
Test 3: Setup block is the correct way to share data with exercises
This test verifies that a setup: true block is executed inside the exercise’s own PGlite instance and is therefore the correct mechanism for preparing data that exercises can access.








Expected result: The exercise block can access setup_ref because it was created inside the exercise’s own PGlite instance via the setup block. The check passes. This contrasts with Test 2, where a global block could not be accessed from an exercise.

Test 1: Isolated exercises do not interfere with each other
This test verifies that two exercises using the same table name do not interfere with each other. Each exercise without an explicit envir gets its own dedicated PGlite instance.
















Expected result: The first exercise contains two rows after execution. The second exercise contains only its own setup row. This confirms that both exercises use separate PGlite instances and do not share state, even when using the same table name.

Expected result: After running both exercises in order, the shared table contains three rows. The second exercise can access rows inserted by the first exercise, confirming that both exercises share the same PGlite instance via the envir label.

title: SQL Environment Tests
section: Test 3: Start Over in a shared environment
text:
Test 3: Start Over in a shared environment
This test verifies the behavior of Start Over when exercises share an environment. Clicking Start Over on one exercise should reset that exercise’s editor content and replay its setup, but the shared environment state may be affected.













Expected result: After running both exercises, ex_start_shared_b shows two rows. After clicking Start Over on ex_start_shared_a and running it again, observe whether ex_start_shared_b still sees the previously inserted row or whether the shared state was affected. This documents the behavior of Start Over in shared environments.

title: SQL Grading Tests
text:
Test 5: __quarto_check_context isolation
This section tests the visibility and isolation of __quarto_check_context across different blocks and environments.

Test 5.1: Exercise block cannot access __quarto_check_context
This test verifies that __quarto_check_context is not visible in the exercise block itself, only during check execution.








Expected result: The exercise block produces the error relation "__quarto_check_context" does not exist. The check itself passes because it runs after the context table is created by the grader.



Test 5.2: Another exercise in the same envir cannot access __quarto_check_context
This test verifies that __quarto_check_context created during one exercise’s check is not visible to another exercise sharing the same envir.














Expected result: ex_ctx_shared_b produces the error relation "__quarto_check_context" does not exist. This confirms that __quarto_check_context is only available during check execution and is not persistent in the shared environment.



Test 5.3: Global block cannot access __quarto_check_context
This test verifies that __quarto_check_context is not visible in the global environment.














Expected result: The global block produces the error relation "__quarto_check_context" does not exist. This confirms that __quarto_check_context is not visible outside of check execution.



Test 5.4: Check code error behavior
This test verifies what happens when the check code itself produces a SQL error.








Expected result: The check produces an error and displays it as negative feedback. The exercise block itself executed successfully.




Test 5.5: user_code in __quarto_check_context reflects last execution
This test verifies that __quarto_check_context.user_code contains the SQL code from the most recent exercise execution.








Expected result: The check passes because user_code contains the INSERT statement from the exercise block. This confirms that __quarto_check_context reflects the most recently executed exercise code.
